### Tutorial 6.2: Calculating Revenue by Item Group and Quarter Using SUMIFS

**Context and objective.** You will use SUMIFS to build a revenue summary table that shows total revenue for each item group in each fiscal quarter. This produces the same output you will later build more efficiently with a PivotTable, but constructing it with formulas first helps you understand the underlying logic of conditional aggregation.

**Prerequisites.** You need the merged InvoiceLines dataset from Chapter 5, with columns for InvoiceDate, ItemGroup, QuantityShipped, LineTotal, and a FiscalQuarter column derived from InvoiceDate.

**Step 1.** Create a new worksheet and name it "RevenueByGroupQtr." In cell A1, type "Revenue by Item Group and Fiscal Quarter" as a title. In cell A3, type "Item Group." In cells B3 through E3, type "Q1," "Q2," "Q3," and "Q4." In cell F3, type "Total."

**Step 2.** In cells A4 through A7, enter the four Charles River item groups. Furniture, Lighting, Textiles, and Accessories.

**Step 3.** Before writing the SUMIFS formula, confirm how fiscal quarters appear in your data. If you added a FiscalQuarter column during the data preparation in Chapter 5, you can reference that column directly. If your data contains only the InvoiceDate, you will need to define the quarter boundaries. For this tutorial, assume the fiscal year aligns with the calendar year and that Q1 covers January through March, Q2 covers April through June, Q3 covers July through September, and Q4 covers October through December.

**Step 4.** In cell B4, enter the SUMIFS formula for Furniture revenue in Q1. With the InvoiceLines table and its FiscalQuarter column, the formula is =SUMIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal], InvoiceLines[ItemGroup], $A4, InvoiceLines[FiscalQuarter], B$3). Note the mixed references. $A4 locks the column reference so you can copy the formula across columns, and B$3 locks the row reference so you can copy it down rows.

**Step 5.** Copy the formula in B4 across columns B through E and down rows 4 through 7 to fill the entire revenue table. The dollar signs in the mixed references ensure that each formula points to the correct item group in column A and the correct quarter label in row 3.

**Step 6.** In column F, enter =SUM(B4:E4) for each row to calculate the annual total for each item group. In row 8, enter =SUM(B4:B7) for each column to calculate the quarterly totals across all item groups.

**Step 7.** Format the revenue values as currency with no decimal places for readability. Apply a bottom border above the totals row and a right border to the left of the totals column to distinguish the summary totals from the detail cells.

**Checkpoint.** Your revenue summary table should show four item groups across four quarters, with row and column totals. The grand total in cell F8 should equal approximately $3,332,300 and should match the sum of all LineTotal values in your source data. If it does not, check that your SUMIFS criteria match correctly and that every row in the source data has a valid ItemGroup and FiscalQuarter value. Common mismatches occur when item group labels contain trailing spaces or when some invoices fall outside the four quarter definitions.

Row headers show the four item groups, column headers show Q1 through Q4 and Total, and cells contain formatted currency values. The formula bar displays the SUMIFS formula for the active cell with mixed references visible.]*

Furniture is the dominant item group across all quarters, and Q4 is the strongest quarter for every group.*

> **[WATCH OUT]**
> A common error when building SUMIFS tables is forgetting to use mixed references. If you write =SUMIFS(InvoiceLines[LineTotal], InvoiceLines[ItemGroup], A4, InvoiceLines[FiscalQuarter], B3) without any dollar signs and then copy the formula, the references will shift in both directions and produce incorrect results. The formula will appear to work without generating an error, but the values will be wrong. Always verify your SUMIFS table by checking that the row and column totals equal the sum of the individual cells, and that the grand total matches the total of the source data.
